title: MPEP 2143 — Examples of Basic Requirements of a Prima Facie Case of Obviousness

extracted.subtask_short: Seven KSR rationales for combining/substituting prior art elements
extracted.subtask_description: Operationalizes the KSR obviousness rationales (A-G) into concrete required-findings tests, with illustrative case contrasts, plus cross-cutting lessons on why finding all claim elements in the prior art is necessary but not sufficient for obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale A — combining known elements per known methods, predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Required findings: (1) all claimed elements are found in the prior art (not necessarily in a single reference); (2) a PHOSITA could have combined the elements using known methods; (3) each element, in combination, retains its separate known function — the results are predictable (not synergistic/unexpected); (4) any additional Graham findings needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: *Anderson's-Black Rock v. Pavement Salvage Co.*: mounting a known radiant-heat burner onto a paving machine chassis was obvious — predictable convenience, not a new function. *United States v. Adams*: combining known magnesium and cuprous-chloride battery electrodes with water activation was NOT obvious because prior art taught such combinations were impractical (art taught away). *Crocs, Inc. v. ITC*: combining a known foam base with known elastic straps was NOT obvious — prior art counseled against foam straps, so the resulting fit was an unpredictable, superior result. Key takeaway: merely finding every claim element somewhere in the prior art is not enough — there must also be a finding that the combined result would have been predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale B — simple substitution of one known element for another
rubrics_metrics.description: Required findings: (1) a prior art device differs from the claim only by substitution of a component; (2) the substituted component, and its function, was known; (3) a PHOSITA could have performed the substitution with predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: *In re Fout* (substituting evaporative distillation for aqueous extraction in decaffeination was obvious; an express suggestion to substitute is not required); *Agrizap v. Woodstream* (substituting a resistive electrical switch for a mechanical pressure switch was a "textbook case," reinforced because both switch types solved the identical dirt/dampness malfunction problem, even though the resistive switch was known from a different device category). Counter-example where it failed: *Eisai v. Dr. Reddy's* — swapping one substituent for a structurally similar one was not obvious because the prior art gave reasons to expect worse properties from the swap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale C — known technique to improve similar devices in the same way
rubrics_metrics.description: Required findings: identification of a "base" device the claim improves, a "comparable" (not identical) device improved by the same technique in the prior art, and a finding that a PHOSITA could apply that known improvement technique to the base device with predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: *In re Nilssen* — using a known cutoff-switch technique (known for protecting one type of inverter circuit) to protect a different but comparable inverter circuit was obvious, because the technique's function transferred predictably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale D — known technique applied to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Required findings: a known base device/method, a known technique applicable to it, and a finding that a PHOSITA would have recognized applying the known technique would yield predictable, improved results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: *Dann v. Johnston* — adding category codes (a known indexing technique) to standard bank check-processing computer systems was obvious. Also *In re Urbanski* — shortening a known enzymatic reaction time within a range taught by a second reference was obvious because both references recognized reaction time as a "result-effective variable" and neither taught away from shortening it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale E — "obvious to try" among a finite set of predictable solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Required findings: (1) a recognized problem or need existed in the art (potentially design need or market pressure); (2) a finite number of identified, predictable potential solutions existed; (3) a PHOSITA could have pursued those known options with a reasonable expectation of success. *KSR*: "When there is a design need or market pressure to solve a problem and there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, a person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue the known options within his or her technical grasp."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where it succeeds: *Pfizer v. Apotex* (amlodipine besylate — only 53 pharmaceutically acceptable anions existed, a small finite set with reasonable expectation of success); *In re Kubin* (a limited, routine set of cloning/sequencing techniques applied to an already-identified target protein). Where it fails: *In re O'Farrell* identifies two failure patterns — varying all parameters with no direction on likely success, or exploring a new/promising general approach with only general guidance toward the particular claimed form. *Takeda v. Alphapharm* (pioglitazone) — prior art disclosed hundreds of millions of candidates generally with no reason to select the specific lead compound, which had a known disadvantageous property. *Ortho-McNeil v. Mylan* (topiramate) — no finite, easily-traversed option set existed; the discovery was serendipitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale F — known work in one field prompting predictable variations elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Supports combining across fields when market/design pressure (not necessarily an explicit textual suggestion) would have prompted the variation, and the resulting variation is predictable to a PHOSITA. Overlaps with the analogous-art "reasonably pertinent" prong and is frequently invoked alongside Rationale B/C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: *Leapfrog Enterprises v. Fisher-Price* (applying modern electronics to prior-art mechanical learning devices was prompted by predictable market/design pressure to modernize).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale G — teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: This preserves the pre-*KSR* TSM approach as one valid rationale among seven, not the exclusive test. An examiner may still point to an explicit or implicit suggestion in the prior art itself to combine or modify references. The suggestion must be specific enough to actually point a PHOSITA toward the claimed combination with a reasonable expectation of success — general encouragement to explore a research area is not equivalent to a specific direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: All elements present in the prior art does not automatically mean obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Under every rationale, presence of all claim elements somewhere in the prior art is necessary but not sufficient; predictability of the combined/substituted/modified result is an independent, separately-required finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away defeats every rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: If the closest reference(s) criticize, discourage, or warn against the specific modification needed to bridge the claim-to-art delta, no rationale can support obviousness on that record.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Ready for improvement" and "recognized problem" require evidence, not assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: A device or process is only "ready for improvement" (Rationale D) or facing a "recognized problem" (Rationale E) if the record shows a PHOSITA would have perceived it that way at the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural similarity alone is not obviousness — need reason to select the lead compound
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural similarity alone (chemical/biotech cases) is not obviousness — there must additionally be a reason to select the particular "lead compound" and a reasonable expectation that modifying it would preserve or improve (not destroy) the relevant properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cf. *Eisai*, *Altana*, *Procter & Gamble v. Teva*. The list of rationales is non-exhaustive; other rationales are permitted as long as the examiner ties factual findings to the ultimate legal conclusion with a "rational underpinning."
